name: Acid egg
short description: The terms acid egg and montejus (or monte, jus) are sometimes used interchangeably to refer to a device with no moving parts formerly used instead of a pump in order to transfer difficult liquids. The principle is that a strong vessel containing the liquid is pressurized with gas or steam, forcing the liquid into a pipe (usually vertical upwards) thereby causing flow. When the liquid has been transferred, the pressure is released and more liquid is put in via gravity.
typical applications: Standards and guidelines for the interpretation of sequence variants: a joint consensus recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Genetics in Medicine, 2015), Global cancer statistics, 2012 (CA A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, 2015), Initial sequencing and analysis of the human genome (Nature, 2001), SwissADME: a free web tool to evaluate pharmacokinetics, drug, likeness and medicinal chemistry friendliness of small molecules (Scientific Reports, 2017), Preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta, analysis protocols (PRISMA, P) 2015: elaboration and explanation (BMJ, 2015)
research-oriented use: 1. Maintaining ultra, high vacuum conditions with Acid egg for surface, science experiments requiring atomically clean substrates. 2. Delivering precise fluid flow rates using Acid egg in microfluidic devices for biological assay development.

name: Acid test
short description: An acid test is a qualitative chemical or metallurgical assay utilizing acid. Historically, it often involved the use of a robust acid to distinguish gold from base metals. Figuratively, the term represents any definitive test for attributes, such as gauging a person's character or evaluating a product's performance.
typical applications: PROTEIN MEASUREMENT WITH THE FOLIN PHENOL REAGENT (Journal of Biological Chemistry, 1951), Global cancer statistics (CA A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, 2011), Short, Term Effects of Nose, Only Cigarette Smoke Exposure on Glutathione Redox Homeostasis, Cytochrome P450 1A1/2 and Respiratory Enzyme Activities in Mice Tissues (Cellular Physiology and Biochemistry, 2013), The CLUSTAL_X windows interface: flexible strategies for multiple sequence alignment aided by quality analysis tools (Nucleic Acids Research, 1997), MEGA X: Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis across Computing Platforms (Molecular Biology and Evolution, 2018)
research-oriented use: 1. A product's performance using Acid test in a research setting, enabling systematic data collection for chemical and molecular sciences studies. 2. Employing Acid test as part of an integrated analytical workflow for comparative analysis and method validation in research.

name: Acid value
short description: In chemistry, acid value (AV, acid number, neutralization number or acidity) is a number used to quantify the acidity of a given chemical substance. It is the quantity of base (usually potassium hydroxide (KOH)), expressed as milligrams of KOH required to neutralize the acidic constituents in 1 gram of a sample. The acid value measures the acidity of water, insoluble substances like oils, fats, waxes and resins, which do not have a pH value.
typical applications: PROTEIN MEASUREMENT WITH THE FOLIN PHENOL REAGENT (Journal of Biological Chemistry, 1951), Short, Term Effects of Nose, Only Cigarette Smoke Exposure on Glutathione Redox Homeostasis, Cytochrome P450 1A1/2 and Respiratory Enzyme Activities in Mice Tissues (Cellular Physiology and Biochemistry, 2013), The CLUSTAL_X windows interface: flexible strategies for multiple sequence alignment aided by quality analysis tools (Nucleic Acids Research, 1997), Coot: model, building tools for molecular graphics (Acta Crystallographica Section D Biological Crystallography, 2004), Standards and guidelines for the interpretation of sequence variants: a joint consensus recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Genetics in Medicine, 2015)
research-oriented use: 1. An increment in the amount of FFAs in a fat or oil sample indicates hydrolysis of triglycerides. 2. Such reaction occurs by the action of lipase enzyme and it is an indicator of inadequate processing and storage conditions.

name: Acid-fastness
short description: Acid, fastness is a physical property of certain bacteria, protozoa, and eukaryotic cells, as well as some subcellular structures, referring to their resistance to decolorization by acids during laboratory staining procedures. Once stained as part of a sample, these organisms can resist the acid and/or ethanol, based decolorization procedures common in many staining protocols, hence the name acid, fast. Historically, acid, fast stains were thought to stain lipids of the cells based on the observed characteristics of cell staining under a wide range of conditions, although the results were limited by the tools available, however as early as 1959 there were observations of how nucleic acids were acid fast.
typical applications: Science and information theory (Journal of the Franklin Institute, 1956), Textile dyeing industry an environmental hazard (Natural Science, 2012), Evaluation of a nutrient starvation model of Mycobacterium tuberculosis persistence by gene and protein expression profiling (Molecular Microbiology, 2002), Cancer, A Biological Approach: I. The Processes Of Control. II. The Significance of Somatic Mutation (BMJ, 1957), Inorganic yellow, red pigments without toxic metals (Nature, 2000)
research-oriented use: 1. Applying Acid, fastness — acid, fastness is a physical property of certain bacteria, protozoa, and eukaryotic cells, as well as some subcellular structures, referring to their resistance to decolorization by acids during laboratory staining procedures — to investigate research questions in biological and life sciences. 2. Employing Acid, fastness as part of an integrated analytical workflow for comparative analysis and method validation in research.

name: Acidophil cell
short description: In the anterior pituitary, the term "acidophil" is used to describe two different types of cells which stain well with acidic dyes. Somatotrophs, which secrete growth hormone (a peptide hormone) Lactotrophs, which secrete prolactin (a peptide hormone) When using standard staining techniques, they cannot be distinguished from each other (though they can be distinguished from basophils and chromophobes), and are therefore identified simply as "acidophils".
typical applications: Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) Activity Score and the Histopathologic Diagnosis in NAFLD: Distinct Clinicopathologic Meanings §Δ (Hepatology, 2010), An experimental model of idiopathic pneumonia syndrome after bone marrow transplantation: I. The roles of minor H antigens and endotoxin (Blood, 1996), Lactobacillus acidophilus LA 1 binds to cultured human intestinal cell lines and inhibits cell attachment and cell invasion by enterovirulent bacteria. (Gut, 1994), Familial Haemophagocytic Reticulosis (Archives of Disease in Childhood, 1952), THE BRAIN, STEM LESIONS IN PARKINSONISM (Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry, 1953)
research-oriented use: 1. Describe two different types of cells which stain well with acidic dyes using Acidophil cell in a research setting, enabling systematic data collection for biological and life sciences studies. 2. Employing Acidophil cell as part of an integrated analytical workflow for quality control and compliance verification.

name: Acid–base extraction
short description: Acid–base extraction is a subclass of liquid–liquid extractions and involves the separation of chemical species from other acidic or basic compounds. It is typically performed during the work, up step following a chemical synthesis to purify crude compounds and results in the product being largely free of acidic or basic impurities. A separatory funnel is commonly used to perform an acid, base extraction.
typical applications: KEGG: Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (Nucleic Acids Research, 2000), Standards and guidelines for the interpretation of sequence variants: a joint consensus recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Genetics in Medicine, 2015), PHENIX: a comprehensive Python, based system for macromolecular structure solution (Acta Crystallographica Section D Biological Crystallography, 2010), A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin (Nature, 2020), An integrated encyclopedia of DNA elements in the human genome (Nature, 2012)
research-oriented use: 1. Phenylamine is first collected in the organic layer, then phenol is collected from the aqueous layer. 2. The green layer in the separatory funnel indicates the organic layer, while the colourless layer indicates the aqueous layer.

name: Acid–base reaction
short description: In chemistry, an acid–base reaction is a chemical reaction that occurs between an acid and a base. It can be used to determine pH via titration. Several theoretical frameworks provide alternative conceptions of the reaction mechanisms and their application in solving related problems; these are called the acid–base theories, for example, Brønsted–Lowry acid–base theory.
typical applications: PROTEIN MEASUREMENT WITH THE FOLIN PHENOL REAGENT (Journal of Biological Chemistry, 1951), KEGG: Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (Nucleic Acids Research, 2000), The M06 suite of density functionals for main group thermochemistry, thermochemical kinetics, noncovalent interactions, excited states, and transition elements: two new functionals and systematic testing of four M06, class functionals and 12 other functionals (Theoretical Chemistry Accounts, 2007), Initial sequencing and analysis of the human genome (Nature, 2001), A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin (Nature, 2020)
research-oriented use: 1. Determine pH via titration using Acid–base reaction in a research setting, enabling systematic data collection for biological and life sciences studies. 2. PH via titration with Acid–base reaction for quantitative analysis and reproducible experimental validation.

name: Acid–base titration
short description: An acid–base titration is a method of quantitative analysis for determining the concentration of Brønsted, Lowry acid or base (titrate) by neutralizing it using a solution of known concentration (titrant). A pH indicator is used to monitor the progress of the acid–base reaction and a titration curve can be constructed. This differs from other modern modes of titrations, such as oxidation, reduction titrations, precipitation titrations, & complexometric titrations.
typical applications: 2016 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (European Heart Journal, 2016), 2018 ESC/ESH Guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension (European Heart Journal, 2018), Better reporting of interventions: template for intervention description and replication (TIDieR) checklist and guide (BMJ, 2014), 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias: lipid modification to reduce cardiovascular risk (European Heart Journal, 2019), In situ click chemistry generation of cyclooxygenase, 2 inhibitors (Nature Communications, 2017)
research-oriented use: 1. 2. # initial pH # pH before the equivalence point # pH at the equivalence point # pH after the equivalence point 1.

name: Aclara Biosciences
short description: Aclara Biosciences, Inc. (also stylized as ACLARA Biosciences) was a medical technology company, focused on developing applications of microfluidics for use in laboratory testing. It was publicly traded on NASDAQ under the symbol ACLA.
typical applications: Carrageenan Is a Potent Inhibitor of Papillomavirus Infection (PLoS Pathogens, 2006), Evolutionary origins of invasive populations (Evolutionary Applications, 2008), Biosensors for environmental applications: Future development trends (Pure and Applied Chemistry, 2004), Adaptive radiation of photosynthetic physiology in the Hawaiian lobeliads: light regimes, static light responses, and whole‐plant compensation points (American Journal of Botany, 2004), Evolutionary Biology for the 21st Century (PLoS Biology, 2013)
research-oriented use: 1. Performing single, cell analysis in droplet, based microfluidic devices using Aclara Biosciences for systems biology research. 2. Developing organs, on, chip models with Aclara Biosciences for pharmaceutical toxicity screening studies.

name: Acoustic Doppler current profiler
short description: An acoustic doppler current profiler (ADCP) is a hydroacoustic current meter similar to a sonar, used to measure water current velocities over a depth range using the Doppler effect of sound waves scattered back from particles within the water column. The term ADCP is a generic term for all acoustic current profilers, although the abbreviation originates from an instrument series introduced by RD Instruments in the 1980s. The working frequencies range of ADCPs range from 38 kHz to several megahertz.
typical applications: 2016 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (European Heart Journal, 2016), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute and Chronic Heart Failure (European Journal of Heart Failure, 2016), Anomalous collapses of Nares Strait ice arches leads to enhanced export of Arctic sea ice (Nature Communications, 2021), 2014 ESC Guidelines on diagnosis and management of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (European Heart Journal, 2014), Recommendations for evaluation of the severity of native valvular regurgitation with two, dimensional and doppler echocardiography (Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography, 2003)
research-oriented use: 1. Three common methods are used to calculate the Doppler shift and thus the water velocity along the acoustic beams. 2. The first method uses a monochromatic transmit pulse and is referred to as "incoherent" or "narrowband".

name: Acoustic angiography
short description: A specific branch of contrast, enhanced ultrasound, acoustic angiography is a minimally invasive and non, ionizing medical imaging technique used to visualize vasculature. Acoustic angiography was first developed by the Dayton Laboratory at North Carolina State University and provides a safe, portable, and inexpensive alternative to the most common methods of angiography such as Magnetic Resonance Angiography and Computed Tomography Angiography. Although ultrasound does not traditionally exhibit the high resolution of MRI or CT, high, frequency ultrasound (HFU) achieves relatively high resolution by sacrificing some penetration depth.
typical applications: 2016 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (European Heart Journal, 2016), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute and Chronic Heart Failure (European Journal of Heart Failure, 2016), 2014 ESC Guidelines on diagnosis and management of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (European Heart Journal, 2014), Recommendations for evaluation of the severity of native valvular regurgitation with two, dimensional and doppler echocardiography (Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography, 2003), Photoacoustic imaging in biomedicine (Review of Scientific Instruments, 2006)
research-oriented use: 1. As acoustic angiography is currently under development, this specific branch of contrast, enhanced ultrasound is not currently used in clinical settings. 2. The majority of the previous work using acoustic angiography has studied angiogenesis in animal models for research purposes.

name: Acoustic droplet ejection
short description: Acoustic droplet ejection (ADE) uses a pulse of ultrasound to move low volumes of fluids (typically nanoliters or picoliters) without any physical contact. This technology focuses acoustic energy into a fluid sample in order to eject droplets as small as a picoliter. ADE technology is a very gentle process, and it can be used to transfer proteins, high molecular weight DNA and live cells without damage or loss of viability.
typical applications: Active Particles in Complex and Crowded Environments (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2016), Controlled drug delivery vehicles for cancer treatment and their performance (Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, 2018), A wearable and highly sensitive pressure sensor with ultrathin gold nanowires (Nature Communications, 2014), Microscale acoustofluidics: Microfluidics driven via acoustics and ultrasonics (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2011), SCoPE, MS: mass spectrometry of single mammalian cells quantifies proteome heterogeneity during cell differentiation (Genome biology, 2018)
research-oriented use: 1. Performing gravimetric analysis of precipitated analytes using Acoustic droplet ejection for quantitative analytical chemistry research. 2. Measuring mass changes during adsorption/desorption experiments with Acoustic droplet ejection for surface chemistry studies.

name: Acoustic emission
short description: Acoustic emission (AE) is the phenomenon of radiation of acoustic (elastic) waves in solids that occurs when a material undergoes irreversible changes in its internal structure, for example as a result of crack formation or plastic deformation due to aging, temperature gradients, or external mechanical forces. In particular, AE occurs during the processes of mechanical loading of materials and structures accompanied by structural changes that generate local sources of elastic waves. This results in small surface displacements of a material produced by elastic or stress waves generated when the accumulated elastic energy in a material or on its surface is released rapidly.
typical applications: Gradient, based learning applied to document recognition (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1998), A comparative risk assessment of burden of disease and injury attributable to 67 risk factors and risk factor clusters in 21 regions, 1990–2010: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2010 (The Lancet, 2012), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (European Heart Journal, 2016), Planck2013 results. XVI. Cosmological parameters (Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2014), Internet of Things for Smart Cities (IEEE Internet of Things Journal, 2014)
research-oriented use: 1. The application of acoustic emission to nondestructive testing of materials typically takes place between 20 kHz and 1 MHz. 2. Unlike conventional ultrasonic testing, AE tools are designed for monitoring acoustic emissions produced by the material during failure or stress, and not on the material's effect on externally generated waves.

name: Acoustic location
short description: Acoustic location is a method of determining the position of an object or sound source by using sound waves. Location can take place in gases (such as the atmosphere), liquids (such as water), and in solids (such as in the earth). Location can be done actively or passively: Active acoustic location involves the creation of sound in order to produce an echo, which is then analyzed to determine the location of the object in question.
typical applications: Gradient, based learning applied to document recognition (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1998), The qualitative content analysis process (Journal of Advanced Nursing, 2008), Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger (Physical Review Letters, 2016), CBTRUS Statistical Report: Primary Brain and Central Nervous System Tumors Diagnosed in the United States in 2006, 2010 (Neuro, Oncology, 2013), Review of deep learning: concepts, CNN architectures, challenges, applications, future directions (Journal Of Big Data, 2021)
research-oriented use: 1. Different methods for obtaining either source direction or source location are possible. 2. Steered response power (SRP) methods are a class of indirect acoustic source localization methods.

name: Acoustic microscopy
short description: Acoustic microscopy is microscopy that employs very high or ultra high frequency ultrasound. Acoustic microscopes operate non, destructively and penetrate most solid materials to make visible images of internal features, including defects such as cracks, delaminations and voids.
typical applications: Minimal information for studies of extracellular vesicles 2018 (MISEV2018): a position statement of the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles and update of the MISEV2014 guidelines (Journal of Extracellular Vesicles, 2018), Review of deep learning: concepts, CNN architectures, challenges, applications, future directions (Journal Of Big Data, 2021), Stochastic resonance (Reviews of Modern Physics, 1998), Neurons Containing Hypocretin (Orexin) Project to Multiple Neuronal Systems (Journal of Neuroscience, 1998), On the Construction and Comparison of Difference Schemes (SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis, 1968)
research-oriented use: 1. The samples imaged by acoustic microscopes are typically assemblies of one or more solid materials that have at least one surface that is either flat or regularly curved. 2. The depth of interest may involve an internal bond between materials, or a depth at which a defect may occur in a homogeneous material.

name: Acoustic mirror
short description: An acoustic mirror is a passive device used to reflect and focus (concentrate) sound waves. Parabolic acoustic mirrors are widely used in parabolic microphones to pick up sound from great distances, employed in surveillance and reporting of outdoor sporting events. Pairs of large parabolic acoustic mirrors which function as "whisper galleries" are displayed in science museums to demonstrate sound focusing.
typical applications: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger (Physical Review Letters, 2016), Review of deep learning: concepts, CNN architectures, challenges, applications, future directions (Journal Of Big Data, 2021), The magical number 4 in short, term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity (Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2001), Internet of Things for Smart Cities (IEEE Internet of Things Journal, 2014), Cavity optomechanics (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2014)
research-oriented use: 1. Louis Science Center, Parkes Observatory in Australia and on the north campus lawn of North Carolina State University. 2. in diameter, is installed facing each other, separated by around a hundred metres (yards).

name: Acoustic paramagnetic resonance
short description: In acoustics, acoustic paramagnetic resonance (APR) is a phenomenon of resonant absorption of sound by a system of magnetic particles placed in an external magnetic field. It occurs when the energy of the sound wave quantum becomes equal to the splitting of the energy levels of the particles, the splitting being induced by the magnetic field. APR is a variation of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) where the acoustic rather than electromagnetic waves are absorbed by the studied sample.
typical applications: Stochastic resonance (Reviews of Modern Physics, 1998), Antiferromagnetic spintronics (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2018), Controlled drug delivery vehicles for cancer treatment and their performance (Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, 2018), Ultrafast optical manipulation of magnetic order (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2010), Magnonics (Journal of Physics D Applied Physics, 2010)
research-oriented use: 1. APR is commonly measured using the pulsed echo technique at high sound frequencies of the order 100 MHz – 100 GHz. 2. Two opposite sides of a studied crystal are mirror polished and made parallel to each other, and a piezoelectric crystal is attached to one side.

name: Acoustic resonance spectroscopy
short description: Acoustic resonance spectroscopy (ARS) is a method of spectroscopy in the acoustic region, primarily the sonic and ultrasonic regions. ARS is typically much more rapid than HPLC and NIR. It is non destructive and requires no sample preparation as the sampling waveguide can simply be pushed into a sample powder/liquid or in contact with a solid sample.
typical applications: Minimal information for studies of extracellular vesicles 2018 (MISEV2018): a position statement of the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles and update of the MISEV2014 guidelines (Journal of Extracellular Vesicles, 2018), On the Construction and Comparison of Difference Schemes (SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis, 1968), Photoacoustic imaging in biomedicine (Review of Scientific Instruments, 2006), Antiferromagnetic spintronics (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2018), Advances in atomic force microscopy (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2003)
research-oriented use: 1. One potential application of ARS involves the rapid and nondestructive identification of drug tablet verification. 2. Currently, there are no unfailing methods to eliminate contaminated or mislabeled products, a process which sometimes results in millions of pills having to be recalled.

name: Acoustic resonance technology
short description: Acoustic resonance technology (ART) is an acoustic inspection technology developed by Det Norske Veritas over the past 20 years. ART exploits the phenomenon of half, wave resonance, whereby a suitably excited resonant target (such as a pipeline wall) exhibits longitudinal resonances at certain frequencies characteristic of the target's thickness. Knowing the speed of sound in the target material, the half, wave resonant frequencies can be used to calculate the target's thickness.
typical applications: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger (Physical Review Letters, 2016), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (European Heart Journal, 2016), Minimal information for studies of extracellular vesicles 2018 (MISEV2018): a position statement of the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles and update of the MISEV2014 guidelines (Journal of Extracellular Vesicles, 2018), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute and Chronic Heart Failure (European Journal of Heart Failure, 2016), Cavity optomechanics (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2014)
research-oriented use: 1. Calculate the target's thickness using Acoustic resonance technology in a research setting, enabling systematic data collection for materials science and engineering studies. 2. Employing Acoustic resonance technology as part of an integrated analytical workflow for quality control and compliance verification.

name: Acoustic rheometer
short description: An acoustic rheometer is a device used to measure the rheological properties of fluids, such as viscosity and elasticity, by utilizing sound waves. It works by generating acoustic waves in the fluid and analyzing the changes in the wave propagation caused by the fluid's rheological behavior. An acoustic rheometer uses a piezo, electric crystal to generate the acoustic waves, applying an oscillating extensional stress to the system.
typical applications: Colloquium: The glass transition and elastic models of glass, forming liquids (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2006), Recent advances in biodegradable polymers for sustainable applications (npj Materials Degradation, 2022), Microcontinuum Field Theories II: Fluent Media (Applied Mechanics Reviews, 2002), Gelatin methacryloyl and its hydrogels with an exceptional degree of controllability and batch, to, batch consistency (Scientific Reports, 2019), Mechanics of human voice production and control (The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 2016)
research-oriented use: 1. Characterizing the flow behavior of complex fluids (polymers, suspensions, biological fluids) using Acoustic rheometer for formulation science. 2. Measuring viscoelastic properties of hydrogels or tissue, mimetic materials with Acoustic rheometer for biomedical engineering research.

name: Acoustic theory
short description: Acoustic theory is a scientific field that relates to the description of sound waves. It derives from fluid dynamics. See acoustics for the engineering approach.
typical applications: Gradient, based learning applied to document recognition (Proceedings of the IEEE, 1998), The qualitative content analysis process (Journal of Advanced Nursing, 2008), Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger (Physical Review Letters, 2016), Planck 2018 results (Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2020), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure (European Heart Journal, 2016)
research-oriented use: 1. Applying Acoustic theory — acoustic theory is a scientific field that relates to the description of sound waves — to investigate research questions in physics and photonics. 2. Employing Acoustic theory as part of an integrated analytical workflow for field, based and in, situ measurement campaigns.

name: Acousto-optic programmable dispersive filter
short description: An acousto, optic programmable dispersive filter (AOPDF) is a special type of collinear, beam acousto, optic modulator capable of shaping spectral phase and amplitude of ultrashort laser pulses. AOPDF was invented by Pierre Tournois. Typically, quartz crystals are used for the fabrication of the AOPDFs operating in the UV spectral domain, paratellurite crystals are used in the visible and the NIR (up to 4 μm) and calomel in the MIR (3–20 μm).
typical applications: Optics and interferometry with atoms and molecules (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2009), Roadmap on structured light (Journal of Optics, 2016), Integrated photonics on thin, film lithium niobate (Advances in Optics and Photonics, 2021), Amplitude and phase control of ultrashort pulses by use of an acousto, optic programmable dispersive filter: pulse compression and shaping (Optics Letters, 2000), Intelligent Image, Activated Cell Sorting (Cell, 2018)
research-oriented use: 1. Traveling acoustic wave induces variations in optical properties, thus forming a dynamic volume grating.

name: Acousto-optical spectrometer
short description: An acousto, optical spectrometer (AOS) is based on the diffraction of light by ultrasonic waves. A piezoelectric transducer, driven by the RF signal (from the receiver), generates an acoustic wave in a crystal (the so, called Bragg, cell). This acoustic wave modulates the refractive index and induces a phase grating.
typical applications: Stochastic resonance (Reviews of Modern Physics, 1998), HerschelSpace Observatory (Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2010), Optics and interferometry with atoms and molecules (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2009), Integrated photonics on thin, film lithium niobate (Advances in Optics and Photonics, 2021), Sensitivity optimization for NV, diamond magnetometry (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2020)
research-oriented use: 1. Characterizing the chemical composition of novel materials by analyzing spectral signatures with Acousto, optical spectrometer to identify functional groups and molecular structures. 2. Monitoring environmental pollutant concentrations in water or air samples using Acousto, optical spectrometer for quantitative trace analysis in environmental science studies.

name: Acousto-optics
short description: Acousto, optics is a branch of physics that studies the interactions between sound waves and light waves, especially the diffraction of laser light by ultrasound (or sound in general) through an ultrasonic grating.
typical applications: Experimental Test of Bell's Inequalities Using Time, Varying Analyzers (Physical Review Letters, 1982), HerschelSpace Observatory (Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2010), Storage of Light in Atomic Vapor (Physical Review Letters, 2001), Generation of Squeezed States by Parametric Down Conversion (Physical Review Letters, 1986), Dynamics of Phononic Materials and Structures: Historical Origins, Recent Progress, and Future Outlook (Applied Mechanics Reviews, 2014)
research-oriented use: 1. Determining the crystal structure and phase composition of newly synthesized materials using Acousto, optics for structural characterization in materials research. 2. Assessing residual stress and crystallite size in thin, film coatings with Acousto, optics for engineering and surface science studies.

name: Acree–Rosenheim reaction
short description: The Acree–Rosenheim reaction is a chemical test used for detecting the presence of tryptophan in proteins. A protein mixture is mixed with formaldehyde. Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to form two layers.
typical applications: Intranasal Concentrations of Orally Administered Flavors (Chemical Senses, 2005), A STUDY OF THE PHYSIOLOGICAL EFFECTS OF ELEMENTAL SULPHUR DUST ON CITRUS FRUITS (PLANT PHYSIOLOGY, 1950), Can a chemical be both readily biodegradable AND very persistent (vP)? Weight, of, evidence determination demonstrates that phenanthrene is not persistent in the environment (Environmental Sciences Europe, 2020), A rapid and low cost sensitive method of on, spot detection of RDX (Cyclonite) (Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research), 2006), Extraction Of Collagen From Fish Orientai Sole Brachirus orientalis Skin And Studying Of Some Chemical Charactristics And Amino Acid Composition (IRAQI JOURNAL OF AQUACULTURE, 2021)
research-oriented use: 1. Detecting the presence of tryptophan in proteins using Acree–Rosenheim reaction in a research setting, enabling systematic data collection for biological and life sciences studies. 2. The presence of tryptophan in proteins with Acree–Rosenheim reaction for quantitative analysis and reproducible experimental validation.

name: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene
short description: Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) (chemical formula (C8H8)x·​(C4H6)y·​(C3H3N)z ) is a thermoplastic polymer, in common use since the 1950s. At room temperature it is an amorphous solid, and has no definitive melting point, due to the varying length of monomer chains, and various degrees of cross, linking. Its glass transition temperature is approximately 105 °C (221 °F).
typical applications: Encyclopedia of polymer science and technology (Choice Reviews Online, 2003), Lignocellulosic biomass: a sustainable platform for the production of bio, based chemicals and polymers (Polymer Chemistry, 2015), Additive manufacturing: scientific and technological challenges, market uptake and opportunities (Materials Today, 2017), Highly oriented carbon fiber–polymer composites via additive manufacturing (Composites Science and Technology, 2014), 50th Anniversary Perspective: RAFT Polymerization—A User Guide (Macromolecules, 2017)
research-oriented use: 1. 2. ABS's light weight and ability to be injection molded and extruded make it useful in manufacturing products such as drain, waste, vent (DWV) pipe systems.

name: Acsensorize
short description: Acsensorize (v.t.), pronounced as ac, sensor, ize, is the act of adding a multitude of dissimilar sensors, generally of a variety of sensing modalities, to an existing system that may or may not already have sensors; acsensorizing (pres. part.); acsensorized (past. part.); acsensorization (n.) is the process of acsensorizing.
typical applications: From total quality management to Quality 4.0: A systematic literature review and future research agenda (Frontiers of Engineering Management, 2023), Quality 4.0 – an evolution of Six Sigma DMAIC (International Journal of Lean Six Sigma, 2022), Quality 4.0 in Digital Manufacturing – Example of Good Practice (Quality Innovation Prosperity, 2023)
research-oriented use: 1. Developing real, time monitoring systems for environmental parameters (e.g., pH, temperature, gas concentration) using Acsensorize in field, deployed sensor networks. 2. Integrating Acsensorize into point, of, care diagnostic devices for rapid biomarker detection in clinical research.

name: Actigraphy
short description: Actigraphy is a non, invasive method of monitoring human rest/activity cycles. A small actigraph unit, also called an actimetry sensor, is worn for a week or more to measure gross motor activity. The unit is usually in a wristwatch, like package worn on the wrist.
typical applications: The Cumulative Cost of Additional Wakefulness: Dose, Response Effects on Neurobehavioral Functions and Sleep Physiology From Chronic Sleep Restriction and Total Sleep Deprivation (SLEEP, 2003), Clinical Guideline for the Evaluation, Management and Long, term Care of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults (Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 2009), Cumulative Sleepiness, Mood Disturbance, and Psychomotor Vigilance Performance Decrements During a Week of Sleep Restricted to 4–5 Hours per Night (SLEEP, 1997), Automatic Sleep/Wake Identification From Wrist Activity (SLEEP, 1992), Digital Twin: Values, Challenges and Enablers From a Modeling Perspective (IEEE Access, 2020)
research-oriented use: 1. Devices used for actigraphy collect data generated by movements. 2. In order to make the data usable for practice and sleep medicine, movements are translated into digital data by actigraphs.

name: Actinides in the environment
short description: The actinide series is a group of chemical elements with atomic numbers ranging from 89 to 102, including notable elements such as uranium and plutonium. The nuclides (or isotopes) thorium, 232, uranium, 235, and uranium, 238 occur primordially, while trace quantities of actinium, protactinium, neptunium, and plutonium exist as a result of radioactive decay and, in the case of neptunium and plutonium, neutron capture of uranium. These elements have much shorter half, lives than the naturally occurring thorium and uranium, and thus are far more radioactive.
typical applications: The Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD): assessing the accuracy of DFT formation energies (npj Computational Materials, 2015), Exploiting single, ion anisotropy in the design of f, element single, molecule magnets (Chemical Science, 2011), Jaguar: A high‐performance quantum chemistry software program with strengths in life and materials sciences (International Journal of Quantum Chemistry, 2013), Chemical treatment technologies for waste, water recycling—an overview (RSC Advances, 2012), ClassyFire: automated chemical classification with a comprehensive, computable taxonomy (Journal of Cheminformatics, 2016)
research-oriented use: 1. Conducting radiotracer studies to map metabolic pathways using Actinides in the environment in biomedics or environmental science. 2. Measuring radioactive decay rates and isotope ratios with Actinides in the environment for geochronology or nuclear physics research.

name: Actinograph
short description: An actinograph is an instrument for measuring or estimating the amount of light available, in terms of its ability to expose photographic film. That is, it measures the actinic or chemical intensity of light, as opposed to radiometric or photometric amount of light. The earliest actinographs were 24, hour recording devices, using a rotating cylinder of photographic paper exposed through a wedged, shaped slit to record a graph of actinic light during the period of a day; hence the graph suffix in actinograph.
typical applications: Detection of dimming/brightening in Italy from homogenized all, sky andclear, sky surface solar radiation records and underlying causes (1959–2013) (Atmospheric chemistry and physics, 2016), Plankton studies in a mangrove environment II: the standing stock and some ecological factors (Boletim do Instituto Oceanográfico, 1965), Estimated monthly average global radiation for Turkey and its comparison with observations (Renewable Energy, 1997), Atmospheric transmissivity: distribution and empirical estimation around the central Andes (International Journal of Climatology, 2004), Behavioral and Electrophysiological Responses of Arhopalus tristis to Burnt Pine and Other Stimuli (Journal of Chemical Ecology, 2001)
research-oriented use: 1. The actinic or chemical intensity of light using Actinograph in a research setting, enabling systematic data collection for chemical and molecular sciences studies. 2. Employing Actinograph as part of an integrated analytical workflow for comparative analysis and method validation in research.

name: Actinometer
short description: An actinometer is an instrument that can measure the heating power of radiation. Actinometers are used in meteorology to measure solar radiation as pyranometers, pyrheliometers and net radiometers. An actinometer is a chemical system or physical device which determines the number of photons in a beam integrally or per unit time.
typical applications: A new sensitive chemical actinometer, II. Potassium ferrioxalate as a standard chemical actinometer (Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 1956), Reference materials for fluorescence measurement (Pure and Applied Chemistry, 1988), Reactive species in non, equilibrium atmospheric, pressure plasmas: Generation, transport, and biological effects (Physics Reports, 2016), Glossary of terms used in photochemistry, 3rd edition (IUPAC Recommendations 2006) (Pure and Applied Chemistry, 2007), Characterizing chain processes in visible light photoredox catalysis (Chemical Science, 2015)
research-oriented use: 1. Characterizing power conversion efficiency and spectral response of novel photovoltaic materials using Actinometer for renewable energy research. 2. Degradation testing of solar cell modules under accelerated aging conditions with Actinometer for reliability studies.

name: Action spectrum
short description: An action spectrum is a graph of the rate of biological effectiveness plotted against wavelength of light. It is related to absorption spectrum in many systems. Mathematically, it describes the inverse quantity of light required to evoke a constant response.
typical applications: PROTEIN MEASUREMENT WITH THE FOLIN PHENOL REAGENT (Journal of Biological Chemistry, 1951), Global cancer statistics (CA A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, 2011), Standards and guidelines for the interpretation of sequence variants: a joint consensus recommendation of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology (Genetics in Medicine, 2015), An integrated encyclopedia of DNA elements in the human genome (Nature, 2012), Global Cancer Statistics, 2002 (CA A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, 2005)
research-oriented use: 1. Applying Action spectrum — an action spectrum is a graph of the rate of biological effectiveness plotted against wavelength of light — to investigate research questions in biological and life sciences. 2. Employing Action spectrum as part of an integrated analytical workflow for comparative analysis and method validation in research.

name: Activated sludge
short description: The activated sludge process is a type of biological wastewater treatment process for treating sewage or industrial wastewaters using aeration and a biological floc composed of bacteria and protozoa. It is one of several biological wastewater treatment alternatives in secondary treatment, which deals with the removal of biodegradable organic matter and suspended solids. It uses air (or oxygen) and microorganisms to biologically oxidize organic pollutants, producing a waste sludge (or floc) containing the oxidized material.
typical applications: Phylogenetic identification and in situ detection of individual microbial cells without cultivation. (Microbiological Reviews, 1995), Principles and potential of the anaerobic digestion of waste, activated sludge (Progress in Energy and Combustion Science, 2008), The ammonia monooxygenase structural gene amoA as a functional marker: molecular fine, scale analysis of natural ammonia, oxidizing populations (Applied and Environmental Microbiology, 1997), Lignocellulosic biomass: a sustainable platform for the production of bio, based chemicals and polymers (Polymer Chemistry, 2015), Application of peroxymonosulfate and its activation methods for degradation of environmental organic pollutants: Review (Chemical Engineering Journal, 2016)
research-oriented use: 1. 25|A generalized, schematic diagram of an activated sludge process. 2.

name: Activation energy asymptotics
short description: Activation energy asymptotics (AEA), also known as large activation energy asymptotics, is an asymptotic analysis used in the combustion field utilizing the fact that the reaction rate is extremely sensitive to temperature changes due to the large activation energy of the chemical reaction.
typical applications: Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task (Perception & Psychophysics, 1974), Advanced capabilities for materials modelling with Quantum ESPRESSO (Journal of Physics Condensed Matter, 2017), The Problem of Pattern and Scale in Ecology: The Robert H. MacArthur Award Lecture (Ecology, 1992), Stochastic resonance (Reviews of Modern Physics, 1998), Soil and Water Assessment Tool Theoretical Documentation Version 2009 (OakTrust (Texas A&M University Libraries), 2011)
research-oriented use: 1. In combustion processes, the reaction rate \omega is dependent on temperature T in the following form (Arrhenius law), :\omega(T) \propto \mathrm{e}^{, E_{\rm a}/RT}, where E_{\rm a} is the activation energy, and R is the universal gas constant. 2. In general, the condition E_{\rm a}/R \gg T_b is satisfied, where T_{\rm b} is the burnt gas temperature.

name: Active cavity radiometer
short description: An active cavity radiometer is an electrically self, calibrating cavity pyrheliometer that can measure total and spectral solar irradiance.
typical applications: The Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) Sensor Package (Journal of Atmospheric and Oceanic Technology, 1998), SOLAR INFLUENCES ON CLIMATE (Reviews of Geophysics, 2010), Bio‐optical properties of oceanic waters: A reappraisal (Journal of Geophysical Research Atmospheres, 2001), LIGO: the Laser Interferometer Gravitational, Wave Observatory (Reports on Progress in Physics, 2009), Glossary of terms used in photochemistry, 3rd edition (IUPAC Recommendations 2006) (Pure and Applied Chemistry, 2007)
research-oriented use: 1. Characterizing power conversion efficiency and spectral response of novel photovoltaic materials using Active cavity radiometer for renewable energy research. 2. Degradation testing of solar cell modules under accelerated aging conditions with Active cavity radiometer for reliability studies.

name: Active optics
short description: Active optics is a technology used with reflecting telescopes developed in the 1980s, which actively shapes a telescope's mirrors to prevent deformation due to external influences such as wind, temperature, and mechanical stress. Without active optics, the construction of 8 metre class telescopes is not possible, nor would telescopes with segmented mirrors be feasible. This method is used by, among others, the Nordic Optical Telescope, the New Technology Telescope, the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo and the Keck telescopes, as well as all of the largest telescopes built since the mid, 1990s.
typical applications: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger (Physical Review Letters, 2016), Quantum cryptography (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2002), Fractional Brownian Motions, Fractional Noises and Applications (SIAM Review, 1968), TheGaiamission (Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2016), ImageJ2: ImageJ for the next generation of scientific image data (BMC Bioinformatics, 2017)
research-oriented use: 1. Complicated laser set, ups and interferometers can also be actively stabilized. 2. A small part of the beam leaks through beam steering mirrors and a four, quadrant, diode is used to measure the position of a laser beam and another in the focal plane behind a lens is used to measure the direction.

name: Active surface
short description: An active surface is a surface of a radio telescope that is under active computer control of its shape. Large radio telescopes (more than 10 m in diameter or length) always bend during operation, due to their enormous weight and the fact that even the strongest materials are not perfectly stiff. This bending, in the range of a few millimetres, does not affect low frequency operation much, but dramatically reduces the efficiency of the telescope at higher frequencies where the wavelengths are comparable to the distortion.
typical applications: R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing (unknown, 2000), Fitting Linear Mixed, Effects Models Using lme4 (Journal of Statistical Software, 2015), SciPy 1.0: fundamental algorithms for scientific computing in Python (Nature Methods, 2020), QUANTUM ESPRESSO: a modular and open, source software project for quantum simulations of materials (Journal of Physics Condensed Matter, 2009), PHENIX: a comprehensive Python, based system for macromolecular structure solution (Acta Crystallographica Section D Biological Crystallography, 2010)
research-oriented use: 1. Performing gravimetric analysis of precipitated analytes using Active surface for quantitative analytical chemistry research. 2. Measuring mass changes during adsorption/desorption experiments with Active surface for surface chemistry studies.

name: Activity coefficient
short description: In thermodynamics, an activity coefficient is a factor used to account for deviation of a mixture of chemical substances from ideal behaviour. In an ideal mixture, the microscopic interactions between each pair of chemical species are the same (or macroscopically equivalent, the enthalpy change of solution and volume variation in mixing is zero) and, as a result, properties of the mixtures can be expressed directly in terms of simple concentrations or partial pressures of the substances present e.g. Raoult's law.
typical applications: The CES, D Scale (Applied Psychological Measurement, 1977), SciPy 1.0: fundamental algorithms for scientific computing in Python (Nature Methods, 2020), Random sample consensus (Communications of the ACM, 1981), A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin (Nature, 2020), COPPER ENZYMES IN ISOLATED CHLOROPLASTS. POLYPHENOLOXIDASE IN BETA VULGARIS (PLANT PHYSIOLOGY, 1949)
research-oriented use: 1. Activity coefficients may be determined experimentally by making measurements on non, ideal mixtures. 2. Use may be made of Raoult's law or Henry's law to provide a value for an ideal mixture against which the experimental value may be compared to obtain the activity coefficient.

name: Activity-based proteomics
short description: Activity, based proteomics, or activity, based protein profiling (ABPP) is a chemoproteomic strategy that employs modular probes to directly assess the functional state of enzymes within complex proteomes. Unlike expression, based proteomics, which measures protein abundance, ABPP provides information about catalytic activity, thereby enabling researchers to distinguish between active and inactive forms of enzymes. This functional perspective has proven valuable for identifying drug targets, mapping ligandable sites, and understanding enzyme regulation in physiological and pathological contexts.
typical applications: An integrated encyclopedia of DNA elements in the human genome (Nature, 2012), The MIQE Guidelines: Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real, Time PCR Experiments (Clinical Chemistry, 2009), Metascape provides a biologist, oriented resource for the analysis of systems, level datasets (Nature Communications, 2019), Bioinformatics enrichment tools: paths toward the comprehensive functional analysis of large gene lists (Nucleic Acids Research, 2008), Comprehensive molecular portraits of human breast tumours (Nature, 2012)
research-oriented use: 1. frame|In, SDS, PAGE|gel ABPP using probes with different fluorophores in the same lane to simultaneously profile differences in enzyme activities ABPP can be analyzed using several complementary detection strategies, each suited to different experimental contexts. 2. These methods generally visualize or enrich the enzyme, probe adduct, enabling qualitative assessment, quantitative comparison, or protein identification by mass spectrometry.

name: Adams clasp
short description: An Adams clasp is a component used to retain a custom, made medical device in the mouth. The clasp functions by engaging the mesiobuccal and distobuccal undercuts of a tooth, typically the maxillary first molar and is used to retain a wide range of devices prescribed in a variety of medical and dental specialties.
typical applications: How important are comprehensive literature searches and the assessment of trial quality in systematic reviews? Empirical study (Health Technology Assessment, 2003), An updated classification of Orchidaceae (Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society, 2015), Mouse LYVE, 1 Is an Endocytic Receptor for Hyaluronan in Lymphatic Endothelium (Journal of Biological Chemistry, 2001), Global Matrix 2.0: Report Card Grades on the Physical Activity of Children and Youth Comparing 38 Countries (Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 2016), Nuclear RNA, seq of single neurons reveals molecular signatures of activation (Nature Communications, 2016)
research-oriented use: 1. Retain a custom, made medical device in the mouth using Adams clasp in a research setting, enabling systematic data collection for biomedical and clinical research studies. 2. Retain a wide range of devices prescribed in a variety of medical and dental specialties with Adams clasp for quantitative analysis and reproducible experimental validation.

name: Adaptive coil combination
short description: Adaptive coil combination is a method used in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to merge signals from multiple receiver coil elements into a single image. A weighted sum of the individual coil images is performed with a different weighting vector m {\displaystyle \mathbf {m} } for each pixel. Each vector m {\displaystyle \mathbf {m} } maximizes the signal, to, noise ratio (SNR) of a region of interest (ROI) around the pixel.
typical applications: TheGaiamission (Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2016), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation developed in collaboration with EACTS (EP Europace, 2016), 2016 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation developed in collaboration with EACTS (European Heart Journal, 2016), The Alzheimer's disease neuroimaging initiative (ADNI): MRI methods (Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging, 2008), Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension: The Task Force for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Respiratory Society (ERS), endorsed by the International Society of Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) (European Heart Journal, 2009)
research-oriented use: 1. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to merge signals from multiple receiver coil elements into a single image using Adaptive coil combination, enabling systematic investigation and quantitative data collection in research studies. 2. Integrating Adaptive coil combination into multi, instrument measurement workflows for comprehensive sample characterization and comparative studies.

name: Adaptive optics
short description: Adaptive optics (AO) is a technique of precisely deforming a mirror in order to compensate for light distortion. It is used in astronomical telescopes and laser communication systems to remove the effects of atmospheric distortion, in microscopy, optical fabrication and in retinal imaging systems (ophthalmoscopy) to reduce optical aberrations. Adaptive optics works by measuring the distortions in a wavefront and compensating for them with a device that corrects those errors such as a deformable mirror or a liquid crystal array.
typical applications: Quantum cryptography (Reviews of Modern Physics, 2002), Fractional Brownian Motions, Fractional Noises and Applications (SIAM Review, 1968), TheGaiamission (Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2016), ImageJ2: ImageJ for the next generation of scientific image data (BMC Bioinformatics, 2017), The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC (Journal of Instrumentation, 2008)
research-oriented use: 1. Ocular aberrations are generally measured using a wavefront sensor, and the most commonly used type of wavefront sensor is the Shack–Hartmann. 2. Ocular aberrations are caused by spatial phase nonuniformities in the wavefront exiting the eye.

name: Adatom
short description: An adatom is an atom that lies on a crystal surface, and can be thought of as the opposite of a surface vacancy. This term is used in surface chemistry and epitaxy, when describing single atoms lying on surfaces and surface roughness. The word is a portmanteau of "adsorbed atom".
typical applications: Surface Plasmon Spectroscopy of Nanosized Metal Particles (Langmuir, 1996), A dimer method for finding saddle points on high dimensional potential surfaces using only first derivatives (The Journal of Chemical Physics, 1999), Adsorbate, substrate and adsorbate, adsorbate interactions of Na and K adlayers on Al(111) (Physical review. B, Condensed matter, 1992), Recent development of two, dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides and their applications (Materials Today, 2017), Transition from “Supercapacitor” to “Battery” Behavior in Electrochemical Energy Storage (Journal of The Electrochemical Society, 1991)
research-oriented use: 1. In 2012, scientists at the University of New South Wales were able to use phosphine to precisely, deterministically eject a single silicon atom onto a surface of epitaxial silicon. 2. This resulting adatom created what is described as a single, atom transistor.
